decisions.quote: Where Spitzer uses a holistic approach, fundamentally a stylistic analysis guided by the guiding principle of the dampening effect, the present study’s method is based on defining formal patterns to be identified in annotated text to identify instances of relevant stylistic patterns. In the terms proposed by the typology mentioned above, this part of the present study would best be called a re-analysis (of data).
decisions.reason: The study re-analyses the same eleven Racine plays examined by Spitzer (1931) using digital linguistic annotations and formal search queries, making the repetition of Spitzer's study a reproduction (re-analysis of the original texts) supplemented by a comparative baseline.

decisions.quote: 24 of those 50 stylistic patterns could be modeled using search queries applied to richly annotated, digital versions of Racine’s plays. The remaining patterns proved to be too complex and/or too much dependent on context to be modeled at this point. Despite this limitation, this approach permits us not only to reproduce and verify some of Spitzer’s findings, but also to extend his investigation by retrieving additional instances of the relevant stylistic patterns and comparing them to the ones he chose to mention.
decisions.reason: Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, so reproducing original numbers was not checked. In the re-analysis of the original 11 Racine plays using formal CQP queries on annotated texts, the 24 modeled patterns verify Spitzer's cited examples and retrieve even more instances in Racine's works (robust), whereas the qualification regarding authorial versus genre distinctiveness relies on a new comparative corpus of 38 contemporary plays.

prior_decisions.quote: Regarding Racine and the Classical Age, it has become apparent that the stylistic patterns identified by Leo Spitzer, and which in the aggregate produce a dampening effect, again according to Spitzer, are even more frequent in Racine’s work than Spitzer showed. In addition, the analysis was able to show that these patterns are present in varying degrees in Racine’s work and in the work of his contemporaries, but without very strong (or statistically significant) differences, for the most part. The dampening effect, if understood as the aggregate use of individual stylistic patterns, is therefore clearly not an authorial signature style, but the mark of an entire literary genre during a certain period, at the very least.
prior_decisions.reason: Because Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, reproducing original numerical outputs was outside the analysis plan (not checked), while the computational re-analysis and comparative evaluation substantively qualify Spitzer's interpretation of the dampening effect as a distinctive Racinian signature style (robustness challenges).
